mitigation_mechanism: Wooded riparian strips act on the water pathway rather than on the crop: they slow the flow of water from the land into receiving water bodies by increasing infiltration, reducing flow velocity and providing temporary storage [ev_flood_hazard_cole20_1], and mature woodland is the more effective form because of its structural complexity and the deadwood it delivers to the watercourse [ev_flood_hazard_cole20_2]. The only field finding runs from removal: in Marqués de Comillas, Chiapas, floods along with the seasonal drying of permanent streams and altered river dynamics were associated with the loss of riparian forest [ev_flood_hazard_meli19_4].
caveats: Nothing in this pool is a measured reduction in flood damage to a farm. The Chiapas finding describes what losing riparian forest was associated with, in a case study, not what establishing a buffer delivers [ev_flood_hazard_meli19_4]; a newly planted strip is not shown here to reduce flooding, and the review's own condition is that mature woodland is the more effective form [ev_flood_hazard_cole20_2], which a new strip is not. The review that states the benefit confines it to moderate flooding and makes effectiveness conditional on the extent, location, age and density of the woodland [ev_flood_hazard_cole20_2]; no source here reports a buffer holding up under a severe or extreme flood. The effect works on water moving into receiving water bodies, so the farm giving up land need not be the place where the benefit lands. The sources are a UK review, temperate and high-income, plus a single upper-middle-income tropical case; there is no low-income evidence and no magnitude anywhere.

mitigation_mechanism: Both findings describe what standing riparian vegetation was already doing, and infer the mechanism from the cost of its removal. In the agriculture-dominated midwestern US, failure to retain riparian vegetation and floodplains in the headwaters resulted in increased water levels downstream during flood events [ev_flood_hazard_osbo93_19]. In Marques de Comillas, Chiapas, floods, the seasonal drying up of permanent streams and alterations in river dynamics have been associated with the loss of riparian forests [ev_flood_hazard_meli19_4]. The implied mechanism is retention and conveyance of flood water in a vegetated headwater floodplain.
caveats: Neither source measured what a restored buffer does: both are framed on vegetation loss, and the Mexican finding is an association recorded in a case study, not an attributed effect [ev_flood_hazard_meli19_4]. No magnitude, return period or flood severity is reported, so nothing can be said about behaviour in a severe or extreme flood — a practice that slows ordinary runoff is not thereby a defence against an extreme event. The benefit described sits downstream of the restored reach [ev_flood_hazard_osbo93_19], which separates who bears the land-use cost from who gains. The pool is a US review of a temperate high-income floodplain and a tropical upper-middle-income case study; no low- or lower-middle-income evidence supports this row.

mitigation_mechanism: A UK review, citing earlier studies second-hand, states that wooded buffers can slow the flow of water from the land into receiving water bodies by increasing infiltration, reducing flow velocity and providing temporary water storage, and that riparian woodland appears particularly valuable to flood defence under moderate flooding [ev_flood_hazard_cole20_1, ev_flood_hazard_cole20_2].
caveats: No class is stated: both units are second-hand statements from a single high-income, temperate review with no magnitude and no measured finding, so the evidence is too thin to say how much a buffer reduces flood losses for farm households. The review adds that effectiveness depends on woodland extent, location, age and density, with mature woodland more effective, so young planted buffers may not deliver it [ev_flood_hazard_cole20_2]. A second independent source, or a measured flood finding, ideally from a LIC/LMIC setting, is what is missing. The effect is off-site, downstream of the buffer, rather than on the adopting farm.

On the agriculture-dominated midwestern floodplain, failure to retain riparian vegetation and floodplains in the headwaters resulted in increased water levels downstream during flood events [ev_flood_hazard_osbo93_19]; in Chiapas, floods, seasonal drying of permanent streams and altered river dynamics were associated with the loss of riparian forests [ev_flood_hazard_meli19_4]. caveats: Neither finding measures a restored buffer, a magnitude or a flood severity; both describe the consequence of clearing [ev_flood_hazard_osbo93_19, ev_flood_hazard_meli19_4], and the Mexican finding is an association in a case study. Both sources are outside the low-income rainfed cropping systems this row would be read for: a temperate high-income US review and a tropical upper-middle-income case study.

mitigation_mechanism: Flood disturbance can break, buckle or uproot buffer plants, and plants with more flexible stems resist and recover better [ev_flood_hazard_cole20_3]. In a US multispecies riparian buffer, willow posts withstood the intense 1993 flooding and caught large logs and bridge planks, although some stems were skinned and did not resprout [ev_flood_hazard_schultz95_3].
caveats: The same US buffer showed no breaching and no evidence of major damage from flood water or floating debris in one of the wettest years on record, so recorded damage was limited to some stems [ev_flood_hazard_schultz95_1, ev_flood_hazard_schultz95_3]. Evidence is one review statement from the UK and one site report from the USA, both high income and temperate, outside the LIC/LMIC target [ev_flood_hazard_cole20_3, ev_flood_hazard_schultz95_1, ev_flood_hazard_schultz95_3].
